rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods and Results report the authors' own laboratory experiments: generation and characterisation of hydrogen nanobubble water (Figure 1), Cu-exposure cytotoxicity assays on Tetrahymena thermophila (Figure 2), in vitro and in vivo ROS removal assays (Figures 3-4), enzyme activity and qPCR (Figures 5-6).
rows.notes: The study is a laboratory toxicology experiment on hydrogen nanobubble water scavenging reactive oxygen species and alleviating copper toxicity in a single-celled ciliate (T. thermophila). It contains no irrigation system, no drip or aerated drip irrigation, no crop, no soil and no measurement of crop yield or quality. It is cited apparently only because it concerns nanobubble water; it provides no evidence that ADI increases crop yield or quality relative to conventional drip.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods and Results report the authors' own laboratory experiments on hydrogen nanobubble water, Cu toxicity to T. thermophila, in vitro/in vivo ROS removal, antioxidant enzyme activity and gene expression (Figures 1-8).
rows.notes: The study does not involve drip irrigation, crops, pests, diseases or pesticide applications. It shows only that hydrogen nanobubble water removes ROS (H2O2, O2-, OH) in vitro and reduces Cu-induced oxidative stress and cell death in a model ciliate. No evidence on reduced pesticide use or pest control under aerated drip irrigation.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). The study is on hydrogen nanobubble water and oxidative stress in a protozoan model organism, not on irrigation technology; both claim rows fail Q2 on technology mismatch.
